analysis.one_liner: Taxes carbon pollution and returns the revenue through infrastructure spending and monthly household rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill would have taxed carbon at $52 per ton and recycled the money into infrastructure, monthly refunds for low-income households, and tax rebates, but it never received a hearing or vote in its 17 months in Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a $52-per-ton tax on the carbon dioxide content of coal, oil, and natural gas, rising faster than inflation each year. The money would go into a trust fund for highways, transit, passenger rail, water systems, broadband, schools, and housing; $7 billion a year would help coal-country workers and communities, and low-income households would get monthly cash refunds while most other households under 350% of the poverty line would get a tax credit. Imports of carbon-intensive goods like steel and cement would face a matching fee so foreign producers could not undercut American ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households come out ahead on paper: anyone at or below 150% of the poverty line (for example, SNAP or SSI recipients) would get a monthly cash refund sized to cover their estimated loss in purchasing power from the carbon tax. Households between there and 350% of the poverty line would get a refundable "Working Families Relief" tax credit. Everyone who uses roads, transit, passenger rail, water systems, broadband, schools, or public housing would benefit from roughly $100 billion a year in dedicated infrastructure funding. Coal miners and their communities would get $7 billion a year for wages, pensions, health benefits, and abandoned-mine cleanup. Domestic steel, cement, aluminum, and glass makers would gain protection from the border fee on imported carbon-intensive goods.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income households and coal communities

how_it_helps.text: Low-income households would get monthly cash refunds estimated to fully cover their loss in purchasing power from the carbon tax, delivered through SNAP-style state agencies with no fees, and the refund would not count as income against any other benefit.

Households with income up to 350% of the poverty line would receive a refundable tax credit, scaled by family size, that shrinks gradually as income rises, so the tax would not fall hardest on working families.

The bill would dedicate the tax revenue to a Build America Trust Fund paying out roughly $100 billion a year for ten years for highways, transit, airports, passenger rail, harbors, clean water and drinking water, rural water systems, broadband, school construction, public housing, and health and energy research, without requiring a new annual appropriation.

Coal-dependent workers and communities would get $7 billion a year for workforce training, pension and health benefits, and abandoned mine reclamation, plus $700 million a year for carbon-capture coal research.

A border fee on imported carbon-intensive goods like steel, cement, and aluminum would match the cost the carbon tax imposes on domestic producers, and exports would get a matching rebate, protecting American manufacturing jobs.
By pricing carbon at $52 per ton and rising, the tax would directly charge fossil fuels for their pollution, cutting carbon dioxide emissions across coal, oil, and natural gas.

analysis.who_pays: The tax is levied on manufacturers, producers, and importers of coal, petroleum products, and natural gas, who would pass most of it through to everyone else as higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, electricity, and carbon-intensive goods. Households above 350% of the poverty line would pay those higher prices with no rebate to offset them, and businesses would absorb the same costs. Fossil fuel companies would face both the tax itself and shrinking demand as their products became more expensive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and households above the rebate limits

drawbacks.text: Energy and consumer prices would rise for everyone. The refund fully offsets households only up to 150% of the poverty line and the tax credit phases out entirely at 350% of the poverty line, so higher-income households and businesses would bear the full cost with no offset.

The bill contains a deficit-neutrality clause: if trust-fund money set aside for the Energy Refund Program falls short in any year, the Treasury must cut every recipient's monthly refund on a pro-rata basis, so the lowest-income households' protection is not guaranteed.

The tax starts at $52 per ton and its annual increase is calculated as if inflation were 6 percentage points higher than it actually is, meaning the levy would grow much faster than prices generally, a steep trajectory an honest supporter would have to defend against gasoline and heating-bill shocks.

Refund amounts depend on a Treasury estimate of purchasing-power losses made each year in consultation with the Energy Information Administration; if the estimate misses, some households would be under- or over-refunded.

The bill creates a large new federally funded program administered by state agencies with 100% federal reimbursement of administrative costs, a permanent administrative apparatus that would need ongoing oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is genuinely progressive: by construction, low-income households are refunded their full estimated loss and middle-income households are partially or fully offset, while the infrastructure and coal-community money is a real, dedicated ten-year commitment rather than a vague promise. The serious costs are on the other side of the ledger: everyone above the rebate thresholds pays the tax straight, the pro-rata refund cut in a shortfall year puts the poorest households' protection at risk, and the 6-point escalation formula makes the tax far more aggressive over time than the headline $52 figure suggests. A fair reading is that the bill trades broad, visible price increases for targeted refunds and a large public investment, with the main design risk falling on the people least able to absorb it if the money runs short.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to eight House committees when introduced in August 2019, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote in any of them, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative John Larson of Connecticut introduced the bill on August 2, 2019, joined by Representatives Norton, Lynch, and Payne as original cosponsors.

It was referred the same day to eight committees, led by Ways and Means, and within days was sent to subcommittees on Aviation, Railroads, Highways and Transit, Water Resources, Energy, and Energy and Mineral Resources.

In the roughly 17 months between introduction and the end of the Congress on January 3, 2021, no committee held a hearing or markup and the bill never came to the House floor; the action history records no step beyond the referrals.
Support never grew beyond 9 of 231 House Democrats cosponsoring, and no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers are better off because the bill died: they never faced the $52-per-ton tax or the border fee on competing imports. Consumers never saw the fuel-price increases, but also never received the refunds, rebates, or infrastructure spending the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided the carbon tax

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was entirely Democratic (9 of 231 House Democrats, no Republicans), but no vote was ever held, so the actual partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: Coal would be taxed at $52 per ton of its carbon dioxide content, directly raising its cost and pushing users toward other fuels. The bill softens the blow for the industry's workforce and towns with $7 billion a year for wages, pensions, health benefits, and mine reclamation, and $700 million a year for carbon-capture coal research, but the companies themselves would shrink.

Petroleum products and natural gas would carry the same per-ton carbon tax at the point of production or import, raising prices and cutting demand. Exporters get a rebate, but domestic sales would bear the full levy.

industries.industry: Domestic steel, cement, aluminum, and glass manufacturers
industries.note: These energy-intensive industries pay more for fuel like everyone else, but the border fee would charge imported carbon-intensive goods an equivalent amount, protecting them from cheaper high-carbon foreign competition. Their interest here runs partly with manufacturing workers and partly as added cost protection that consumers ultimately pay for.

Roughly $100 billion a year in trust-fund money for highways, transit, rail, water systems, broadband, schools, and housing would flow to construction and design firms, with a qualifications-based selection rule for architecture and engineering contracts over $1 million. The work is a public good, but the money is earmarked without further appropriation, locking in the spending channel.

The bill dedicates $61 billion a year plus the Highway Trust Fund shortfall to highways and transit and over $6 billion a year to passenger rail including the Northeast Corridor, a durable funding stream that current gas-tax receipts do not provide.
